A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Jigsaw++, with the same central method and main experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Breaking Bad and PartNet, including reconstruction metrics, missing-piece tests, assembly evaluations, and parameter ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds alternative-generation comparisons, metric-distribution analysis, and qualitative FantasticBreaks results.

M1.justification: The coordinate-to-color mapping, LEAP/DINOv2 representation, joint latent rectified flow, and retargeting procedure remain unchanged. The conditional generator is an added comparator, while Appendix E explains the assembly workflow already illustrated by the original matching experiment.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on real-world, two-piece FantasticBreaks objects absent from Breaking Bad, using the Breaking Bad-trained model (Appendix F, Figure 11). This extends coverage from synthetic fracture and CAD-part data to real scanned fragments, although the added evidence consists only of several qualitative examples.

E2.justification: Appendix A and Figures 2 and 7 add inversion-then-generation without retargeting and a conditional generator fine-tuned with partial-assembly input tokens. These directly test alternatives to the central retargeting strategy; the existing assembly and completion comparators are retained.

E3.justification: The added comparisons introduce a control using the same generator parameters and inversion settings without retargeting, plus conditional fine-tuning. FantasticBreaks adds a transfer-testing protocol using the Breaking Bad-trained model. Existing splits, metrics, training budgets, and missing-piece settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a direct test of retargeting's necessity, analysis of conditional generation's behavior, per-example metric distributions, and qualitative transfer to real fragments (Appendices A, D, and F). These substantially broaden analysis beyond the retained sampling/noise ablations and missing-piece tests.

E5.justification: Figure 9 newly reports violin distributions of Chamfer distance, precision, and recall, exposing variation across examples beyond the aggregate tables. Existing plus/minus entries remain unchanged; no new seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests are specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds conditional-generation results of 4.8 × 10^-3 Chamfer distance, 46.3% precision, and 50.6% recall, alongside new control, distribution, and real-fragment findings. Tables 1 and 2 change their Chamfer-distance multiplier from 10^-2 to 10^-3 while retaining the numerical entries and rankings. This changes reported magnitudes, not demonstrated same-setting performance; Section 6.2 still quotes the old missing-piece value of 2.0 × 10^-2.

T1.justification: The problem definition, coordinate mapping, rectified-flow equations, retargeting objective, and metric formulas are mathematically unchanged. Neither version provides additional theorems or proofs; the expanded mapping discussion is explanatory.

C1.justification: The abstract drops the claim that the learned shape prior is category-agnostic, and Section 4 changes the encoder description to category robust. The principal claims about complete-shape generation, retargeting, and compatibility with existing assembly methods remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 interprets conditional generation as favoring smoothing and completion over correcting misplaced parts, and expands limitations to spurious geometry arising from probabilistic generation. However, its new claim that conditional precision falls below the input conflicts with the reported 46.3% versus Table 1's 45.6% Jigsaw input precision.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 now specifies that retargeting uses Jigsaw outputs for Breaking Bad and DGL outputs for PartNet, and that the Jigsaw-trained model is tested on SE(3) outputs without additional fine-tuning. Appendix A documents the new comparator implementations. Existing hyperparameters, hardware, runtimes, and access links are retained.

R1.justification: Section 4 newly credits Sridhar et al. and Wang et al. for coordinate-to-color mappings, locating novelty in their application to 3D generation. References supporting conditional generation and FantasticBreaks are also added, while the main related-work organization and positioning remain stable.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the introduction and mapping explanation, expands limitations, adds appendix subsections, and updates affiliation and acknowledgement text. The main section sequence and much of the original prose remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch to two columns, Table 2's panels become vertically stacked, and Figures 2 and 7 expand their comparisons. Figure 6 gains revised failure illustrations; new figures show metric distributions, the assembly workflow, FantasticBreaks, and the existing matching experiment. Original Figures 9 and 10 are retained as Figures 12 and 13.

improvement.justification: The added method-specific controls, real-fragment examples, training disclosures, and more precise attribution modestly strengthen evidence and transparency. The gain is limited by small qualitative transfer coverage and reporting inconsistencies: revised Chamfer-distance units disagree with retained prose, and the new conditional-baseline interpretation misstates its precision relative to the input. The core method and unresolved practical matching limitation remain unchanged.
